Flag Outlier Cells by Median Absolute Deviation

Source: R/flagQC.R
flagQC.Rd

Marks cells whose QC metrics sit an unusual distance from the rest of the data, using the median absolute deviation (MAD) rather than a fixed cutoff. For each metric a centre and spread are estimated, a cell is flagged if it falls more than nmads MADs from the centre, and the result is written back as a logical metadata column. Nothing is subset or removed – flagging and filtering are kept separate so the flags can be inspected, and cross-tabulated against sample or cell type, before any cells are dropped.

Usage

flagQC(
  obj,
  metrics = c(nFeature_RNA = "both", nCount_RNA = "both"),
  nmads = 3,
  bound = c("both", "lower", "higher"),
  log = TRUE,
  group_by = NULL
)

Arguments

obj

A single Seurat object carrying the metrics to be flagged, typically the output of diagnoseQC().

metrics

Metadata columns to flag on. Either an unnamed character vector of column names, which all take the function-level bound, or a named vector of column = bound pairs, which set the bound per metric. The two forms can be mixed: c("nCount_RNA", pctMito = "higher") flags counts using bound and mitochondrial content on the high side only.

nmads

Number of MADs from the median at which a cell becomes an outlier. Must be a single positive number. 3 (the default) is the conventional choice; 2.5 is more aggressive, 5 keeps all but the extremes.

bound

Default tail to flag, applied to every metric not given its own bound in metrics. One of "both" (the default), "lower" or "higher". See Choosing a bound.

log

Estimate the median and MAD on a log2 scale. TRUE by default, which is what count metrics want. See The log transform.

group_by

Discrete metadata column within which to estimate thresholds, so that each cell is judged against its own group rather than against the whole object. NULL (default) estimates one global threshold per metric; "Ident" estimates one per sample. See Where the thresholds come from.

Value

The input object, with one logical metadata column added per metric, named <metric>_<nmads>_<bound>_outliers. TRUE marks an outlier; cells whose metric is NA, whose group_by value is NA, or whose group was skipped stay NA. The column name does not record group_by, so re-running the same metric with different grouping overwrites the previous flags rather than sitting alongside them.

A summary is stored in obj@misc$flagQC as a data frame, one row per metric per group, with columns:

metric, bound, nmads, scale

What was asked for, and whether the estimate was made on the "log2" or "identity" scale.

group_by, group

The column grouped on and the level this row describes, both NA when thresholds were estimated globally.

center, lower, upper

The median and the two thresholds, on the metric's own scale. The threshold for a tail that was not flagged is NA, not an unenforced number.

n_lower, n_upper

Cells flagged by each threshold, again NA for a tail that was not flagged. The two are disjoint, so where both apply they sum to n_flagged.

n_flagged, pct_flagged, n_missing, n_cells

Totals within the group, where n_missing counts cells the metric was NA for and so could not be judged either way.

column

The metadata column written, or NA for a group that was skipped.

Re-running on the same object appends to that table rather than replacing it, so it stays a record of every flag column present. Rows describing a column that is being overwritten are replaced.

Details

MAD-based thresholds adapt to the data. A hard cutoff carried between experiments discards good cells from a low-depth run and keeps bad ones from a deep run; a threshold derived from the data's own distribution does neither. The cost is that it assumes most cells it is estimated from are good – the median and MAD are computed over all of them – so on a badly failed sample it will happily call the failure normal and flag the survivors.

Where the thresholds come from

group_by decides what "the rest of the data" means, and it is the most consequential argument here:

NULL (default)

One global threshold per metric, estimated across every cell in the object. Right for a single sample, and for a merged object whose samples were captured and sequenced together.

"Ident"

A separate threshold per sample – seuratFrom10x() sets Ident to the sample name. Right whenever sequencing depth or cell recovery varies between samples, which is the usual case. A global cutoff on such an object flags most of the shallowest sample and almost none of the deepest, regardless of whether either actually failed.

any other metadata column

A separate threshold per level of that column: a capture batch, a 10x lane, a tissue. Group by the technical variable you want the threshold to absorb.

Grouping is not free. Each group is judged only against itself, so a uniformly bad sample looks fine from the inside and a group with few cells gives an unstable estimate. Groups with fewer than three cells carrying the metric, or where over half the cells share one value, are skipped rather than given a meaningless threshold; they are named in a warning and appear in the summary table with NA thresholds. The two views are worth comparing – if per-sample and global flags disagree sharply, the disagreement is itself the finding.

Choosing a bound

Which tail matters depends on the metric, so the bound is set per metric rather than globally:

"lower"

Only cells below the threshold. The right choice for nFeature_RNA and nCount_RNA, where the low tail is empty droplets and dying cells but the high tail is largely real, well-captured cells.

"higher"

Only cells above it. The right choice for pctMito, where high is bad and low is not.

"both"

Either tail. Useful for count metrics when doublets are the concern, since the high tail is where they sit.

The log transform

Count metrics are right-skewed, which drags the median up and inflates the MAD, so log = TRUE (the default) estimates the centre and spread on a log2 scale. Thresholds are transformed back before they are applied, reported and stored, so the values in the summary table are always on the metric's own scale and can be compared against it directly. If a metric contains zeroes the transform becomes log2(x + 1) and the back-transform compensates; negative values cannot be log-transformed at all, and are an error rather than a silent NaN.

Set log = FALSE for metrics that are already roughly symmetric, such as log10GenesPerUMI or a percentage that does not pile up against zero.

See also

diagnoseQC(), which calculates the metrics this flags on.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
seurat <- diagnoseQC(seurat, organism = "mmu")

# one global threshold per metric
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, c(nCount_RNA = "lower", pctMito = "higher"))

# the same, but each sample judged against itself
seurat <- flagQC(
    seurat,
    metrics  = c(nCount_RNA = "lower", nFeature_RNA = "lower", pctMito = "higher"),
    group_by = "Ident"
)

# per-sample thresholds and counts
seurat@misc$flagQC[, c("metric", "group", "lower", "upper", "n_flagged")]

# which samples lose the most cells?
qc <- seurat@misc$flagQC
with(qc, tapply(pct_flagged, group, max))

# group by a technical variable instead
seurat <- flagQC(seurat, "nCount_RNA", bound = "lower", group_by = "capture_batch")

# nothing has been removed yet -- look first
table(seurat$Ident, seurat$pctMito_3_higher_outliers)

# then filter on whichever flags you trust
flags <- grep("_outliers$", colnames(seurat@meta.data), value = TRUE)
keep  <- !Reduce(`|`, seurat@meta.data[flags])
seurat <- seurat[, which(keep)]
} # }
